tagline: South from the canoe capital on an old railroad bed.
intro: Wally Road leaves Loudonville, which calls itself the Canoe Capital of Ohio for the liveries along the Mohican River, and runs south through Mohican River country on the bed of the old Toledo, Walhonding Valley and Ohio railway, known as the Wally. It is a short road, about eight miles, past an 1882 barn and a bank barn of the 1890s with 22 louvers to let the air through.
It ends at Greer, which was a stop on that railroad. In its heyday the hamlet kept two hardware stores, two schools, a feed mill and a dance hall.

moments.title: Loudonville
moments.text: Laid out in 1814 and named for James Loudon Priest, the village lies about two miles northeast of where the Black Fork and Clear Fork join to make the Mohican.

moments.title: Walnut Grove School
moments.text: A one-room schoolhouse of the late 1800s that held classes until 1920, when the small schools were folded into districts, and was restored in 2002.

moments.title: Greer
moments.text: The hamlet's post office and its dance hall shared one building of about 1920, and one house here came from Sears, Roebuck as a kit in 1913.
